claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation is controlled by the dynamic balance between mechanical removal and chemical reformation of a protective passive oxide layer.
The rate at which mechanically removed oxide reforms governs both wear and corrosion.
The baseline high-entropy alloy can form a passive oxide film under ambient conditions.
Increasing chromium content enhances the alloy's re-passivation kinetics.
Changing only chromium content isolates passive-film reformation as the cause of differences between the alloys.
Tribological contact intermittently breaches the passive film.
Breaching the passive film exposes fresh metal.
Fresh metal exposed in a corrosive environment undergoes metal dissolution.
Faster passive-film reformation shortens the duration for which fresh metal remains exposed.
Shorter exposure of fresh metal limits corrosive attack.
Faster re-passivation reduces the opportunity for abrasive wear mechanisms to operate.
The higher-chromium alloy should have lower total tribo-corrosion degradation than the lower-chromium baseline.
The higher-chromium alloy should exhibit less mechanical material loss than the baseline.
The higher-chromium alloy should exhibit lower anodic dissolution than the baseline.
The prediction should hold in chloride environments that permit effective oxide reformation when wear is slow enough for re-passivation to keep pace.
The prediction may fail when wear removes oxide faster than it can reform.
The prediction may fail under chemical conditions that suppress oxide formation.
XPS or EIS can be used to monitor oxide-film thickness and reformation rate during the comparison.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as changing only chromium so that passive-film reformation is isolated, but the uncertainty field acknowledges that other alloying effects are not fully isolated. Changing chromium also necessarily requires a compensating compositional adjustment unless the exact normalization strategy is specified.
